title: Overemployed: How I Secretly Work Multiple Full-time Jobs (and you can too)
description:
Overemployed. Working 2 jobs or more at the same time. How is this possible? In this video we'll answer how you can become overemployed and optimize every second for working 2 full time jobs at the same time.

It seems like I missed blacking out a few peoples eyes. Who did I miss?

Storyyyy time:
---------------

I was sitting on the bed in what my mom called “the shittiest Airbnb in existence”, an attack my dad did not take lightly. He booked it. 

Despite the decrepit half renovated state, the most important phone call of my life happened in that house.
 
“Hi {Mister E}" the caller said "We are pleased to extend an offer to you and would like to start you at $84,500.”

I listened intently but said nothing. 

The speaker continued, “I know this is lower than what you get now but I have been approved to give you a conditional raise in three months," He said. "normally we wait a full year.” 

That's what I was waiting for. An hour later I received the offer letter and signed it.

The first thing I did was take out a piece of paper.

At my current job with Terrill Binch I was making $119,000 a year. Or $9,916/month. After taxes: $7,136.

The new job was offering me $88,500, they initially offered $62,000 but I negotiated them up. Monthly this was $7,376/month. After taxes: $5,526.

Then I added the two after tax numbers together. $207,500. That was my new salary. At 22 years old.

This would be my ticket to financial freedom. 

I stepped out of the room wanting to scream with joy. I made eye-contact with my parents then walked into the kitchen. They couldn't know.

My double life had begun. I was now overemployed.

---------------

Prompts:

For Linkedin Banner:

"You are a LinkedIn strategist. Your job is to write my LinkedIn headline. Most people just write boring headlines like: ‘Product Manager at X.’ I don’t want that. I want something clickable, personality-driven, keyword-rich, and clear on who I serve.
Use up to 220 characters. Show personality, make it easy to skim, communicate value fast, and weave in relevant industry keywords so my profile is searchable.
Examples I like:• I Help People Land Amazing Jobs Without Applying Online // Need Help With Your Job Search? Let’s Talk• Helping clients build and implement simple, effective financial planning strategies to manage risk | Girl Dad x4• I don’t usually stalk profiles, but when I do I probably have a career opportunity for you. Let’s find out• Making Talent Count by Connecting Dots and Building Brighter Futures• Helping B2B Sales Executives 10x Pipeline Growth | Real Time Data | Lead Generation | Automate List Building• Award-winning Executive Career Coach | Showing you how to build a career so good it will leave employers drooling over you
Guidelines:• Write 3 headline variations in different tones (professional, approachable, bold/fun)• Show who I help and the value I bring• Include relevant keywords for my role and industry so I appear in search results• Avoid corporate fluff and jargon• Make it feel human and memorable
My role is: [INSERT ROLE]My audience is: [INSERT WHO YOU HELP]My value is: [INSERT RESULT/WHAT YOU HELP THEM DO]My important keywords are: [INSERT KEYWORDS]
Now, write my LinkedIn headline."


For LinkedIn About:
"You are a LinkedIn strategist. Transform my profile/resume into a compelling About section that follows this 3-part structure:
Do not include dashes or emojis.
Part 1: Strong Intro (first 3 lines – the hook)• State my field and years of experience.• Share the specific value I bring to companies.• Include one metric if possible.• Make it interesting enough that readers want to click 'see more.'
Part 2: Proof Points (1 short paragraph)• Highlight 2–3 specific achievements that showcase my skills.• Use action verbs + clear results + metrics when possible.• Match these proof points to the types of roles I want next.
Part 3: What Excites Me (forward-looking close)• Share the kind of work that energizes me (without saying 'looking for opportunities').• Paint a picture of my ideal role, project, or industry.• Add one personal touch (a hobby, sport, or interest) to make me relatable.
Optimization Rules:• Naturally weave in 3–5 industry keywords so I appear in searches.• Max Characters is 2,600.• Write only in first person ('I help…'), never third person.• Avoid fluffy buzzwords unless they’re backed by proof.• Make it conversational but professional. Short sentences, varied structure.• No bullet points or lists in the final output. Write it like a story with natural paragraph breaks."

Are they perfect? No. But they help you not stare at a blinking cursor.

The prompt for Job Descriptions:
For this Job Description: Paste job description

You are a resume tailoring analyst. I'm giving you my resume and ONE job description I'm applying to. Pull the keywords that matter for tailoring this resume to this specific job. This is analysis only do NOT rewrite my resume.

{how_ats_works}

- ATS parses sections (summary, skills, experience) and matches the JD's weighted requirements. Required qualifications matter most; preferred/nice-to-have matter less.

- Modern ATS accept semantic equivalents, terms do NOT need to appear verbatimto count. "Drove sprint planning" can satisfy "sprint facilitation."

- Keyword stuffing and unnatural comma-list padding hurt readability and recruiter trust. One natural mention in the right section beats repetition.

- So the goal is real coverage of what the role needs, not exact-string mirroring.

{how_ats_works}

STEP 1 — Frame it

State the role as "Title @ Company." In one line, give a rough read of how well

the resume already aligns with this JD (strong / partial / weak).

STEP 2 — What the JD actually wants

List the JD's key requirements as keywords/terms, separated into:

- Required (must-haves, stated as required qualifications)

- Preferred (nice-to-haves)

Order each by how central it is to the role.

STEP 3 — Already covered

Keywords/terms the JD wants that the resume ALREADY supports, including via

semantic equivalents, not just exact matches. For each, note briefly where the resume shows it. Split into:

- Exact-match terms (the resume uses the same named tool/framework/cert)

- Covered by equivalent (the resume shows the skill under different wording)


STEP 3 is the answer to "what do I already have." STEP 4 is "what to change."

STEP 4 — Tailoring opportunities

JD keywords NOT currently surfaced in the resume that the candidate can plausibly defend, because the resume shows an adjacent or same-category skill. Then also list out the skills or keywords that are not listed and would be harder to defend, this will be up to the discretion of the applier.

Rank the defensible opportunities by priority, highest first. Priority = how central the term is to the role × how easily the resume can defend it. This way, if there's only time for a couple of edits, I know which to make first.

OUTPUT

1. Role label + alignment read

2. JD requirements (Required / Preferred)

3. Already covered (exact-match / covered by equivalent)

4. Tailoring opportunities (with the evidence that justifies each)

title: How Overpowered a Second Job Really Is (The Math)
description:
I remember sitting in a diner. The kind where the waitress calls you "hun", the booths are duct-taped and the ketchup bottles need a firm slap. 

My bacon cheeseburger arrived. It smelled like heaven.
But I couldn’t taste a thing. 
I was staring at my napkin. 

Six months from graduating college. I had a job offer. And not just for any job, my dream job. Merrill Lynch. “Wall Street.” Just shy of six figures.

But the napkin didn’t care about dreams.
Sprawled out in chicken scratch was the sad truth. 
$94.5K salary 
$3K/month expenses
8%/year return

It would take me 20+ years to reach financial freedom. Hell, even at 10% returns it takes a lifetime. 

There had to be a better way.
And lucky for me, it took less than a year to find it:
Overemployment. 
My loophole. 
My escape hatch.

Because life’s too short to grind for 20 years just to breathe. 

P.S. I’m finally home after Houston  New Orleans  Philly.
Only U.S. city left on my list is Atlanta.
And honestly? Nothing beats slipping back into a well-oiled routine.
